units.name: Naming Words and Doing Words
units.summary: Nouns and verbs, and how to find them in a sentence.

topics.name: Nouns and Verbs
topics.summary: Finding the naming word and the doing word in a sentence.

objectives.text: Find the naming words in a sentence.
Find the doing word in a sentence.
Use a test to check whether a word is a noun or a verb.

keyTerms.definition: A naming word. A person, a place, an animal or a thing.
A doing word. It tells what someone or something does.
A group of words that tells a whole idea.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body:
Words do different jobs in a sentence.

You will learn about naming words and doing words.

You will learn a test for telling them apart.

sections.heading: Naming words
sections.body:
A NOUN is a naming word.

It names a person, a place, an animal or a thing.

    person:  boy, teacher, mother, nurse
    place:   school, market, river, village
    animal:  goat, bird, fish, dog
    thing:   cup, book, chair, mango

Here is a test. Can you put "a" or "the" in front of it and does it still sound right?

    the goat    ✓ works → goat is a noun
    the run     ✗ does not work → run is not a noun

That test is not perfect, but for words like these it works well.

sections.heading: Doing words
sections.body:
A VERB is a doing word. It tells what someone or something DOES.

    run, eat, sing, write, sleep, carry, laugh

Here is a test. Can you put "I" in front of it?

    I run     ✓ works → run is a verb
    I sing    ✓ works → sing is a verb
    I goat    ✗ does not work → goat is not a verb

Every sentence needs a verb. Without one, nothing is happening and the sentence is not finished.
sections.example:
Finding both in a sentence.

    The farmer carries a heavy basket.

First find the naming words. Who or what is this about?

    farmer  — a person → noun
    basket  — a thing → noun

Now find the doing word. What is happening?

    carries — that is what the farmer does → verb

So: farmer and basket are nouns. Carries is the verb.

Try another:

    My sister sings in the market.

    Nouns: sister, market
    Verb: sings

Notice "heavy" and "my" are neither. Not every word is a noun or a verb — those two do other jobs.

sections.heading: Why this helps you
sections.body:
This is not just naming things for the sake of it.

When you write a sentence and it feels wrong, it is very often because the verb is missing.

    The boy under the tree.        ← no verb. Not finished.
    The boy sat under the tree.    ← verb added. Now it is a sentence.

If you can find the verb, you can check your own writing.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
For each sentence, name the nouns and the verb.

1. The dog barked loudly.

2. My mother cooks rice.

3. The children walked to school.

4. Is "market" a noun or a verb? Use the test.

5. This is not a sentence: "The big goat near the river." What is missing?

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• A noun is a naming word: person, place, animal or thing.
• A verb is a doing word.
• Test a noun by putting "a" or "the" in front.
• Test a verb by putting "I" in front.
• Every sentence needs a verb.

questions.question: In "The dog barked loudly", which word is the verb?
questions.explanation: The verb is the doing word — what is happening. The dog barked, so "barked" is the verb. "Dog" is a noun, a naming word. "Loudly" tells you HOW it barked, which is a different job again.

questions.question: Is "market" a noun or a verb?
questions.explanation: Use the test. Can you say "the market"? Yes, that sounds right, so it is a noun — it names a place. Now try the verb test: "I market" does not sound right, so it is not a doing word.

questions.question: What is missing from this: "The big goat near the river."?
questions.explanation: There are plenty of naming words — goat, river — but nothing is HAPPENING. The verb is missing, so the idea is not finished. Add one and it becomes a sentence: "The big goat drank near the river."
